# Matrix Spaces and Rank

- [A matrix has four fundamental subspaces](#a-matrix-has-four-fundamental-subspaces)
- [One reduction exposes the structure](#one-reduction-exposes-the-structure)
- [Column and row bases come from different matrices](#column-and-row-bases-come-from-different-matrices)
- [Free variables build a basis for the null space](#free-variables-build-a-basis-for-the-null-space)

## A matrix has four fundamental subspaces {#a-matrix-has-four-fundamental-subspaces}

For an $m\times n$ matrix $\mat{A}$:

| Space | Definition | Lives in |
|---|---|---|
| $\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})$ | span of the columns of $\mat{A}$ | $\reals^m$ |
| $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})$ | solutions of $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{0}$ | $\reals^n$ |
| $\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A})$ | span of the rows of $\mat{A}$ | $\reals^n$ |
| $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})$ | solutions of $\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}\vct{y}=\vct{0}$ | $\reals^m$ |

::: {.key-point}
Always identify the ambient space before comparing subspaces
:::

## One reduction exposes the structure {#one-reduction-exposes-the-structure}

Use one example throughout, recalling
[pivots and free variables from {{< meta decks.d01.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#eliminate-and-organize-with-pivots):

$$
\mat{A}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&1&3\\
2&4&0&4\\
1&2&2&4
\end{bmatrix}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\mat{R}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&0&2\\
0&0&1&1\\
0&0&0&0
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Pivot columns: $1$ and $3$

Free variables: $x_2$ and $x_4$

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})=2
$$

::: {.notes}
Subtract twice the first row from the second and the first row from the third
to get $(0,0,-2,-2)$ and $(0,0,1,1)$. Keep the latter as pivot row, eliminate
the former, then subtract the pivot row from the first row. This gives the
displayed reduced matrix.
:::

## Column and row bases come from different matrices {#column-and-row-bases-come-from-different-matrices}

A basis for the column space uses pivot columns of the [original]{.alert} matrix:

$$
\left\{
\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}
\right\}
$$

A basis for the row space uses nonzero rows of the [reduced]{.alert} matrix:

$$
\left\{
\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0&2\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}0&0&1&1\end{bmatrix}
\right\}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Row reduction preserves the row space but generally changes the column space
:::

## Free variables build a basis for the null space {#free-variables-build-a-basis-for-the-null-space}

From $\mat{R}\vct{x}=\vct{0}$,

$$
x_1=-2x_2-2x_4,
\qquad
x_3=-x_4
$$

Therefore

$$
\vct{x}
=x_2\begin{bmatrix}-2\\1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}
+x_4\begin{bmatrix}-2\\0\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

and

$$
\dim(\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}))=2
$$

::: {.key-point}
Each free variable contributes one independent null-space direction
:::

# Rank and Solution Sets

- [Rank-nullity counts inputs](#rank-nullity-counts-inputs)

## Rank-nullity counts inputs {#rank-nullity-counts-inputs}

For an $m\times n$ matrix $\mat{A}$,

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})
+\operatorname{nullity}(\mat{A})=n
$$

In the example,

$$
2+2=4
$$

Interpretation:

- rank counts independent input directions that remain visible
- nullity counts independent input directions sent to zero

::: {.key-point}
Rank-nullity accounts for every direction in the input space
:::

---

### Rank-nullity predicts solution sets {#rank-nullity-predicts-solution-sets}

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Compare two $3\times5$ matrices: $\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})=2$ and $\operatorname{rank}(\mat{B})=3$
<span class="exsub">Find each nullity</span>
<span class="exsub">Could either system $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ or $\mat{B}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ have exactly one solution?</span>
<span class="exsub">Which system is solvable for every $\vct{b}\in\reals^3$?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Use $\mat{A}$ on the board and leave $\mat{B}$ for students. The nullities
are $3$ and $2$. Neither system can have exactly one solution when consistent,
because each null space contains nonzero directions. Only $\mat{B}$ has rank
$3$ and hence column space $\reals^3$, so only $\mat{B}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ is
solvable for every $\vct{b}\in\reals^3$.
:::

# Orthogonal Pairs

- [The four spaces pair through orthogonality](#the-four-spaces-pair-through-orthogonality)

## The four spaces pair through orthogonality {#the-four-spaces-pair-through-orthogonality}

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$,

$$
\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A})^\perp
=\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})
\qquad\text{inside }\reals^n
$$

$$
\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})^\perp
=\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})
\qquad\text{inside }\reals^m
$$

The dimensions balance:

$$
\dim(\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A}))=\dim(\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A}))=r
$$

$$
\dim(\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}))=n-r,
\qquad
\dim(\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}))=m-r
$$

---

### Worked example: see both orthogonal pairs {#worked-example-see-both-orthogonal-pairs}

Take the rank-one matrix

$$
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\2&4&0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Inside $\reals^3$:

$$
\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0)^{\mathsf T}\},
\qquad
\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})=\{(-2s,s,t)^{\mathsf T}:s,t\in\reals\}
$$

Their dot product is $-2s+2s=0$

Inside $\reals^2$:

$$
\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)^{\mathsf T}\},
\qquad
\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{span}\{(-2,1)^{\mathsf T}\}
$$

Their dot product is $-2+2=0$

::: {.key-point}
Row–null orthogonality and column–left-null orthogonality use different
ambient spaces
:::

---

### Practice: orthogonality and ambient spaces {#practice-orthogonality-and-ambient-spaces}

Let

$$
\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Find the two orthogonal pairs
<span class="exsub">Find a basis for $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{B})$; check its dot products with both rows</span>
<span class="exsub">What are $\operatorname{Col}(\mat{B})$ and $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{B}^{\mathsf T})$?</span>
<span class="exsub">Check the dimension sums in $\reals^3$ and $\reals^2$</span>
<span class="exsub">Does it make sense to take the dot product of a row-space vector with a column-space vector here?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The null space has basis {(-1,-1,1)^T}; its dot product with each row is
zero. The column space is R^2 and the left null space is {0}. The dimension
sums are 2+1=3 and 2+0=2. Row-space vectors have three coordinates and
column-space vectors have two, so their dot product is not defined.
:::

# Rank Factorization and the Left Null Space

- [Rank factorization keeps the independent columns and rows](#rank-factorization-keeps-the-independent-columns-and-rows)
- [Find the left null space](#find-the-left-null-space)

## Rank factorization keeps the independent columns and rows {#rank-factorization-keeps-the-independent-columns-and-rows}

For the example, take the pivot columns of $\mat{A}$ and the nonzero rows of
$\mat{R}$:

$$
\mat{C}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
2&0\\
1&2
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{R}_r=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&0&2\\
0&0&1&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then

$$
\mat{A}=\mat{C}\mat{R}_r
$$

::: {.key-point}
The columns of $\mat{C}$ form a column-space basis; the rows of $\mat{R}_r$
form a row-space basis
:::

---

### Check the factorization column by column {#check-the-factorization-column-by-column}

Write the columns of $\mat{C}$ as $\vct{c}_1,\vct{c}_2$

The columns of $\mat{R}_r$ give the coefficients, just as in
[the matrix product by columns in {{< meta decks.d01.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#matrix-matrix-multiplication-collects-dot-products):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vct{a}_1&=\vct{c}_1 &
\vct{a}_2&=2\vct{c}_1\\
\vct{a}_3&=\vct{c}_2 &
\vct{a}_4&=2\vct{c}_1+\vct{c}_2
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\mat{C}\mat{R}_r$ rebuilds all four columns of $\mat{A}$

::: {.key-point}
In $\mat{A}=\mat{C}\mat{R}_r$, $\mat{C}$ stores independent columns and
$\mat{R}_r$ tells how to combine them
:::

---

### Practice constructing rank factorizations {#practice-constructing-rank-factorizations}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>For each matrix $\mat{M}$ below, find $\mat{C}$ and $\mat{R}_r$ with $\mat{M}=\mat{C}\mat{R}_r$
<span class="exsub">$\displaystyle\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\\1&2&1\end{bmatrix}$</span>
<span class="exsub">$\displaystyle\mat{D}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2&3\\2&1&4&7\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</span>
:::

For each factorization, identify bases for the row and column spaces

::: {.notes}
For $\mat{B}$, use columns $1$ and $3$:
$\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\mat{R}_r=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$.
For $\mat{D}$, use columns $1$ and $2$:
$\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\mat{R}_r=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2&3\\0&1&0&1\end{bmatrix}$.
The columns of each $\mat{C}$ and rows of each $\mat{R}_r$ give the requested
bases.
:::

## Find the left null space {#find-the-left-null-space}

For the running example, solve $\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}\vct{y}=\vct{0}$

The independent column equations are

$$
y_1+2y_2+y_3=0,
\qquad y_1+2y_3=0
$$

Taking $y_3=2$ gives $\vct{y}=(-4,1,2)^{\mathsf T}$

$$
\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})
=\operatorname{span}\{(-4,1,2)^{\mathsf T}\}
$$

This vector is perpendicular to both columns of $\mat{C}$

---

### One matrix supports several basis questions {#one-matrix-supports-several-basis-questions}

For $\mat{B}$ on the practice slide:

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Complete the picture of its four fundamental subspaces
<span class="exsub">Find bases for $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{B})$ and $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{B}^{\mathsf T})$</span>
<span class="exsub">Check that your left-null vector is perpendicular to both columns of $\mat{C}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Compare the four dimensions with rank–nullity</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
For $\mat{B}$, a null-space basis is $\{(-2,1,0)^{\mathsf T}\}$, and a
left-null basis is $\{(-1,-1,1)^{\mathsf T}\}$. Each is orthogonal to the
appropriate row or column basis. The dimensions are $2,1,2,1$ for column,
null, row, and left null, respectively.
:::

# What the Structure Buys Us

- [A basis turns an abstract problem into a matrix problem](#a-basis-turns-an-abstract-problem-into-a-matrix-problem)
- [A well-chosen basis can simplify an operator](#a-well-chosen-basis-can-simplify-an-operator)

## A basis turns an abstract problem into a matrix problem {#a-basis-turns-an-abstract-problem-into-a-matrix-problem}

Suppose $T:V\to W$ preserves linear combinations:

$$
T(c\vct{u}+d\vct{v})=cT(\vct{u})+dT(\vct{v})
$$

Choose a basis $\mathcal{B}$ for $V$ and a basis $\mathcal{C}$ for $W$

Then some matrix $\mat{M}$ satisfies

$$
[T(\vct{v})]_{\mathcal{C}}
=\mat{M}[\vct{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Matrices are coordinate representations of linear transformations
:::

---

### Worked example: differentiation is a matrix {#worked-example-differentiation-is-a-matrix}

Let $D:\mathbb{P}_2\to\mathbb{P}_1$ send $p$ to $p'$

Use $\mathcal{B}=(1,t,t^2)$ for the input and $\mathcal{C}=(1,t)$ for the output

$$
D(1)=0,
\qquad D(t)=1,
\qquad D(t^2)=2t
$$

Their output coordinate vectors become the columns:

$$
\mat{M}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix},
\qquad [D(p)]_{\mathcal{C}}=\mat{M}[p]_{\mathcal{B}}
$$

For $p=2-3t+5t^2$,

$$
\mat{M}\begin{bmatrix}2\\-3\\5\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}-3\\10\end{bmatrix}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p'=-3+10t
$$

::: {.key-point}
Apply the map to each input basis vector; put its output coordinates in a column
:::

---

### Practice: evaluate a polynomial with a matrix {#practice-evaluate-a-polynomial-with-a-matrix}

Let $T:\mathbb{P}_2\to\reals^2$ be

$$
T(p)=\begin{bmatrix}p(0)\\p(1)\end{bmatrix}
$$

Use $\mathcal{B}=(1,t,t^2)$ and standard output coordinates

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Construct and interpret the matrix of $T$
<span class="exsub">Find $T(1)$, $T(t)$, and $T(t^2)$; make them the columns of $\mat{M}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Use $\mat{M}$ to evaluate $p=2-3t+5t^2$ at both points</span>
<span class="exsub">Find a nonzero polynomial sent to zero; explain why two values cannot identify every quadratic</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The columns are (1,1)^T, (0,1)^T, (0,1)^T, so M=[[1,0,0],[1,1,1]].
For p=2-3t+5t^2, the output is (2,4)^T. Its null space consists of coefficient
vectors (0,-s,s)^T: the corresponding polynomials are s(t^2-t).
The rank is two and nullity one. Adding any multiple of t^2-t leaves both
sampled values unchanged. T preserves linear combinations by pointwise
evaluation.
:::


## A well-chosen basis can simplify an operator {#a-well-chosen-basis-can-simplify-an-operator}

Different bases give different matrices for the same linear transformation

The [next deck]({{< meta decks.d07.file >}}) asks whether a basis can make a square matrix diagonal:

$$
\mat{P}^{-1}\mat{A}\mat{P}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\lambda_1&&0\\
&\ddots&\\
0&&\lambda_n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

The basis vectors must be directions whose spans are preserved by $\mat{A}$

::: {.key-point}
Eigenvectors are basis candidates adapted to the action of a matrix
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- Reduction reveals bases for row, column, and null spaces
- Rank–nullity counts visible and null input directions
- Row/null and column/left-null spaces form orthogonal pairs
- Rank factorization separates independent columns from their combinations
- Bases turn abstract linear maps into matrices

# How Far We Have Come

- [Systems and Matrices]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}) established elimination, pivots, and linear combinations
- [Euclidean Spaces]({{< meta decks.d05.file >}}) gave geometric meaning to vectors and solution sets
- [Vector Spaces and Span]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}) extends those operations to matrices, polynomials, and functions
- [Bases and Coordinates]({{< meta decks.d06b.file >}}) makes representations unique and counts independent directions
- This deck connects bases and dimension to matrix spaces and linear maps
